newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end weaker in quiet trade.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end weaker in quiet trade.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended mostly lower Tuesday in quiet trade, ahead of Wednesday's OTC (over-the-counter) options expiry.

"Nothing much will happen in the first hour tomorrow either until we get the OTC options expiry out of the way," North American Equity Services floor trader John Geraghty said. "Both gold and silver are likely to focus on $390 and $5.30 strike prices, respectively," he said.
"But then we have an early close in metals trading Friday, ahead of the Labor Day Movement, its a quiet week."
COMEX December gold ended down $0.50 an ounce at $394.00, after trading in a narrow $394.70-393.60 range, with total volume estimated at 15,000 lots.
In New York bullion trade, spot gold was quoted at $388.80/389.20 near the close, from a London afternoon fix Tuesday at $388.80, and a New York close Monday at $389.20/389.70.
COMEX September silver ended down 1.6 cents at $5.317, after trading in a $5.355-5.290 range on total estimated volume of 30,000 lots.

"With the September silver contract becoming deliverable at the end of this week, and the New York market facing a three day holiday weekend when London and other markets will remain open, prices may come off later in the week," one analyst said.

Open interest in the September silver contract stood at 157.8 million ounces late last week, compared to registered COMEX stocks of 107.6 million ounces. Another 42.7 million ounces of silver are held in COMEX licensed bank depositaries but are not registered with the COMEX at present.
"Precious metals are entering a better seasonal period as the summer slowdown comes to an end," Merrill Lynch's New York based senior futures strategist Bill O'Neill said in a weekly report.
"While we are not particularly bullish on precious metals, we have raised them to neutral from underweight within our commodity weightings."
NYMEX October platinum ended down $0.50 an ounce at $405.30 while NYMEX December palladium, now the active contract, ended up $1.40 at $127.75.
"The approaching first delivery date of the NYMEX palladium contract, with low registered stocks, should be supporting palladium prices, if not moving them higher," one analyst said.
Open interest in September palladium, which becomes deliverable next week, stood at 387,500 ounces late last week, compared to only 12,000 ounces of palladium registered against NYMEX positions.
